questions.prompt: What does a byte ratio of large outbound with minimal inbound most suggest?
questions.explanation: Normal browsing is small request, large response. Inverting that asymmetry -- lots leaving, little returning -- is the shape of data being sent out rather than retrieved.

questions.prompt: Why is a JA3 fingerprint more durable than an IP or domain indicator?
options: It hashes the client's TLS Client Hello parameters, which are a property of the tooling rather than the destination -- so changing infrastructure does not change it
JA3 is stored permanently in DNS
questions.explanation: Because the fingerprint reflects the TLS library and its configuration, it sits at the tool level of the Pyramid of Pain rather than the trivially-changed infrastructure levels.

questions.prompt: Why is PowerShell's Invoke-WebRequest User-Agent a useful indicator?
options: It is randomly generated on each request
Its default string announces WindowsPowerShell explicitly, identifying the client library from the log alone
It is identical to Chrome's User-Agent
It is never sent over the network
questions.explanation: Malware frequently uses HTTP library defaults, and those defaults -- python-requests, curl, WindowsPowerShell -- are distinctive enough to flag directly.

questions.prompt: Why is destination rarity across a fleet a useful triage signal?
options: A destination contacted by exactly one host among thousands warrants more attention than one contacted by everyone -- prevalence ranking finds what signatures miss
questions.explanation: Prevalence-based ranking surfaces anomalies without needing a prior signature, complementing rather than replacing signature matching.
